name: Southeast Face
beta: The south face is accessed from Spire Col at 7,760 feet. Route climbs class 2-3 scrambling to a class 4 chimney, then traverses class 3 ledges on the southeast face. Final pitch involves friction slab climbing (class 5.6) or alternate cracks left of the slab. Route-finding to the crux can be challenging. The summit horn is extremely exposed with only room for one person at a time; rope belays required for final exposed sections. Descent via two 60-meter rappels to scree.
overview: Spire Point (8,264 ft) is a sharp granite tower on Itswoot Ridge in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, between the Dana Glacier (east) and Spire Glacier (northwest), along the classic Ptarmigan Traverse. Its summit is famously tiny — room for only one climber at a time — with roughly 1,000+ vertical feet of exposure below the west-side ledges. Most Ptarmigan Traverse parties skip the technical summit block since it adds real 4th/5th-class climbing to an already committing traverse, but as a dedicated objective from Downey Creek it's one of the best short alpine rock outings in the range.

current.approach: Start at the Downey Creek Trailhead (end of FR 26/Suiattle River Road, elev. ~1,450'). Follow the Downey Creek Trail (#792) roughly 6.5 miles of gentle, well-graded old-growth forest walking — recent Forest Service work has added boardwalks and new log bridges — to Sixmile Camp and the final log crossing of Bachelor Creek at about 2,400'. From the north side of that crossing, pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path: it starts as a distinct boot-track climbing steeply beside the creek, then eases into switchbacks. Expect brushy, overgrown sections (salmon berry and vine maple) through the 4,000' meadows; the path fords Bachelor Creek again near a campsite, then climbs an avalanche chute on switchbacks before ducking back into trees on climber's left. Around 5,900' the path tops out on the forested ridge above Cub Lake — descend ~500' on steep switchbacks to the lake (good camping), skirt its north shore, and continue to Itswoot Ridge, where a stream draining the Spire Point basin gives a reliable camp/water source at roughly 6,400'. This is the natural high camp for the route (car-to-camp is already ~12-13 miles and 5,000'+ of gain). From camp, hike north up Itswoot Ridge staying on talus on its west (left) side near the stream to bypass rock towers directly above camp; the ridge crest itself is only walkable in short gentle sections. You'll hit permanent snow before Spire Col (7,760'): either climb moderate ~30° snow straight up to the col, or skirt around the left edge of the snowfield on rock. From the col, contour/climb east on talus and broken ledges roughly 400-500' to the base of the southwest face, where the route starts up loose talus into a short (~30') Class 4 chimney. Rope up for the exposed Class 4-5.5 face/chimney climbing above. Hazards: creek fords on Bachelor Creek can be swift in early season, the Bachelor Creek path is brushy and easy to lose, the avalanche chute holds snow late and is exposed to slide activity into early summer, and the final approach to the col crosses glacier-remnant snow that firms up icy in morning — an axe and possibly crampons are standard kit into midsummer.
approach_variant_names: Bachelor Creek, Itswoot Ridge and Spire Col
current.descent: Descend the same southwest face line rather than a separate walk-off. From the tiny, exposed summit horn, parties typically belay the last person down/back from the highest ledge (3rd ledge below the true summit) using slings around the horn as an anchor, then set up rappels from that ledge system rather than the summit itself for more working room. The standard sequence is two rappels of roughly 28-30 meters each — done with a single 60m rope doubled (not two full 60m raps) — down natural sling/webbing anchors (no bolts reported): the first rappel drops to an anchor just above the Class 4 chimney passed on the way up, and the second rappel from there reaches easy talus at the base of the chimney/face. From there, downclimb and reverse the talus/ledges back to Spire Col, then retrace the approach: down the snow/talus to Itswoot Ridge, around Cub Lake, down the Bachelor Creek path, and out the Downey Creek Trail. Watch for loose rock in the chimney and on the ledges (this is broken alpine granite, not a clean crack system), confirm sling anchors are sound/not sun-bleached before weighting them, and back up questionable webbing with your own if in doubt. Because the approach and descent share the same brushy, routefinding-heavy Bachelor Creek path, budget real time and daylight for the reversal — parties commonly camp at Itswoot Ridge or Cub Lake both nights rather than pushing the whole thing car-to-car.
current.detailed_rack: Small to medium nut set covering sizes 0.5-1.5 inches, plus one or two variable-width cams in the 1-2 inch range. Specialized protection for wide cracks not typically required. Bring slings for natural anchors and rappel setup (natural horn anchors used on descent). Consider one 60-meter rope for rappelling and one for climbing belay.
rack: Two 60m ropes (or one 60m doubled) for rappel
current.pro_needs: Light gear only — the technical difficulty is short (5.6) and mostly about managing exposure and loose rock rather than sustained protection; a few cams/nuts and sling material for rappel anchors is sufficient.
bivy: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
current.rope_note: Remote Dome Peak-area summit; south/southwest face is a 5-pitch 5.6 (low-5th-class) rock route reached via glacier approach. Light trad rack plus glacier travel gear for approach.

name: Spontaneous Distraction
beta: Pitch 1 climbs face moves protected by 3 bolts above a left-trending overlap (5.10a); pitch 2 climbs past two bolts to a crack (5.10a) with a traverse right at the third bolt; pitch 3 is a sport-style pitch with a hard start (5.10a) easing into 5.7-5.8 face climbing; pitch 4 finishes on fun 5.6-5.7 cracks.
overview: A four-pitch, partly-bolted 5.10 route beside Spontaneity Arête, combining a couple of well-protected face/crack pitches with easier finishing cracks.

current.approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line.
approach_variant_names: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, then the gully paralleling the arete
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the route itself using a single 70m rope for pitches 1-2; a 70m rope does not reach from the trees directly above pitch 3's last bolt, so that rappel needs an intermediate station off to the side. Alternatively, parties finishing higher on the peak can rappel down from Spontaneity Arête's descent line to reach the gully near this route.
current.detailed_rack: A standard rack to about 2 inches, plus 6-8 quickdraws for the bolted sections (3 bolts on pitch 1, 2 bolts on pitch 2, more on the pitch 3 sport pitch); extra runners help manage rope drag on the wandering sections. Consider replacing worn webbing noted at the pitch 3 anchor.
rack: Single 70m rope (single-rope rappel of entire route)
current.pro_needs: Mostly bolt-protected low down with some gear placements higher; a standard rack plus quickdraws covers it.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
current.rope_note: One 70m rope is sufficient to rappel the entire route.

name: Spraying Mantis
beta: Fully bolted 100 ft (30 m) sport pitch rated 5.10b/c. The FA party (Wylie Moreshead) recommends starting left of the bolt line and straddling the low nose feature cheval-style rather than pulling straight onto it, keeping the rope managed on the inside leg to avoid an awkward twist. 12 bolts lead to chains at the top.
overview: Alpine sport climb at Sofa King Buttress in The Citidel area.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
current.descent: This is a single-pitch, fully bolted sport route with a chain lower-off anchor at its top; there is no walk-off. Thread/clip the chains and lower the full length of the route (a 60 m rope gives ample margin on this ~30 m line) back to the base.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 12 bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor. No trad gear needed. A 60 m rope is enough to lower off the full ~30 m pitch.
current.pro_needs: Sport rack only — 12 quickdraws (plus 1-2 extra for the anchor). No natural/trad protection required or possible.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route of about 30 m; a single 60 m rope lowers off the chain anchor.

name: Southwest Scramble
beta: Approach the peak from Park Creek campground by ascending a loose talus slope, bearing left toward a cirque below the towers. Route-finding requires staying on the correct gully (right-side route preferred over left). Traverse a ledge across the backside of the southern tower with Class 3-4 moves and occasional exposure. Navigate a slight overhang with a squeeze-through section (Class 3), then traverse the summit tower's backside to a small spur. Final approach involves either climbing a 15-foot Class 4 solid face or wrapping around the left side on Class 3 blocks to reach the summit register. Slings are in place near the summit for rappel anchors.
overview: Storm King is a rugged, remote satellite peak just southwest of Mount Goode in North Cascades National Park's Stephen Mather Wilderness, and one of Washington's 'Bulger List' 100 highest summits. It has no easy access from any direction — approaches run roughly 13 to 20+ miles one-way via Thunder Creek, Cascade Pass/Park Creek Pass, or the Stehekin/Park Creek corridor, making it one of the farthest Top-100 peaks in the state from a trailhead. Most parties combine it with Mount Goode (Northeast Buttress or Southwest Couloir) from a shared high camp. The summit looks straight across upper Park Creek at Buckner, Logan, and Goode.

current.approach: Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek in the North Cascades and is one of the range's most remote 'Bulger/Top 100' summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Mount Goode's south side. The most common line is the Thunder Creek approach: from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20, follow the Thunder Creek Trail (an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail) about 13 miles with only ~600 ft of gain to the McAllister Creek confluence — McAllister Camp (~mile 6) is a common night-one camp. Continue past Junction Camp (~mile 9.5) and Skagit Queen Camp (~mile 13.5) to Thunder Basin Camp (~mile 16.5), then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple miles beyond and follow it up through meadows to Park Creek Pass. Two alternate approaches reach the same basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek from SR-20 (camp at Rainbow Lake, ~9 mi and 2,700 ft of gain), or a southern approach via boat/shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass from the south. All three meet on the Park Creek trail: from the Thunder Creek side, cross Park Creek Pass and descend the trail on its south side; from Stehekin, climb the same trail about two miles above the Two Mile camp (~3,400 ft). Near 4,100 ft the trail crosses a large washout of whitish rock, and the climbers' path leaves the trail a few minutes beyond it at a small cairn. It climbs the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, then trends climber's left through heather, meadow and game trails; above about 6,500 ft the ground turns rocky and cairns mark a Class 2-3 path to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From that basin, traverse snow and talus bearing climber's left for roughly a mile to reach the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers — an ice axe and even crampons are worth carrying into August for lingering snow on this traverse, and it's easy to drift off-line in poor visibility. From the cirque, ascend a long, very loose talus/scree slope on the path of least resistance toward the southwest gully system below the summit rocks; this slope is the approach's main hazard — expect rockfall onto parties below and unstable footing, so helmet up here and space out.
approach_variant_names: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
Stehekin and the Park Creek trail
Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin valley
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line. From the notch/crack area just below the true summit, most parties downclimb the ~15-ft crux crack and the exposed Class 4 ledge just below it. Some instead rappel off the fixed slings (in-situ tat/webbing — inspect it and back it up before committing) back to the ledge on the north side; even with a 60 m rope, expect to downclimb some Class 3 terrain. From the ledge, cross back through the right-most notch and descend the loose talus and scree slope to the cirque. From the base of the talus, traverse back to the basin below Goode and descend the cairned climbers' path and the burned ridge to the Park Creek trail just past the big washout, then continue via whichever of the three approach trails (Thunder Creek, McAlester Pass/Rainbow Creek, or Park Creek/Stehekin) matches your itinerary. Loose rock is the dominant descent hazard from the summit all the way down through the talus — keep helmets on and parties tight until well below the scree.
current.detailed_rack: No rock gear required for the scramble.
current.pro_needs: A scramble with one short technical crux rather than a multi-pitch rock route — a few small cams/stoppers and slings are enough to rig a hand line on the ledge traverse and the summit rappel.
bivy: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail

name: Summertime
beta: P1 follows bolts at 5.10 to chains, then trends left past additional anchor sets. The next section is a corner with traditional gear and a slab. The standout crux pitch is bolted with small trad gear, trending up-right through corners and over a roof (5.11c) to an anchor, after which easier 5.10 slabby climbing leads to the top of the cliff.
overview: The crag's namesake and longest route: a 5-pitch, Grade II trad/sport line that wanders along the line of least resistance up the tallest formation, with a bolted-plus-small-gear crux roof pitch (5.11c) partway up.

current.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until about midday in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
current.descent: Chain anchors at several points along the route let parties lower or rappel pitch by pitch, and the crux pitch ends at an anchor. Above it the easier final pitch runs to the top of the cliff with no fixed descent from there, so plan to come back to the anchors and rappel.
current.detailed_rack: Bolted low down, but bring a small trad rack (small cams and wires) for the corner sections and the crux roof pitch, plus 12+ quickdraws and a 60-70m rope.
current.pro_needs: Mostly bolted; bolts plus small trad gear on the crux pitch, and mixed gear and bolts above — bring a light trad rack in addition to draws.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds

name: North Face
beta: Roughly 2,000 vertical feet of water and alpine ice: a lower ramp of about 600 ft of WI2-3 water ice, then a first snowfield, a second snowfield, and an AI2 exit step to reach the upper mountain. The FA party found excellent neve and abundant ice but only carried two titanium ice screws, supplementing protection with knifeblade pitons in compact rock between ice sections. Because the line only forms briefly, it has almost no repeat trip-report history and is considered one of the Cascades' 'forgotten' ice testpieces.
overview: A rarely repeated, sustained alpine ice line up a series of runnels and couloirs just right of the true summit on Summit Chief's north side, with unusually continuous ice climbing for a Cascade route.

current.approach: Approach from the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley (North Bend side): drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (NF-56) to its plowed/drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance (about 1 mile in the FA party's case) into the valley. Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing multiple braids of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River (the crux of the approach in high water), then climb to a camp below the north face. The FA party's full approach from vehicle to camp took about 6.5 hours.
approach_variant_names: Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley in spring, river braids and a camp below the face
current.descent: From the summit area, downclimb neve on the southwest aspect to the top of a snow gully, then make two 30m rappels down the gully to regain lower-angle terrain and return toward the approach basin/camp.
current.detailed_rack: A light ice rack supplemented by rock gear: the FA party carried just two titanium ice screws (rationed carefully across the sustained ice) plus knifeblade pitons for protection in compact, thin sections of rock between ice bands.
current.pro_needs: Screw placements are limited by thin/compact ice in places; supplement with knifeblade pitons in the intervening rock bands.

name: South Route
beta: From a high camp near Vista Lakes or Summit Chief Lake, parties traverse off-trail north across Vista Ridge to Summit Chief Pass and into the peak's southeast basin. Snowfields below the southeast face are climbed via a snow finger to gain the south ridge (the first, left-most finger dead-ends at a notch, requiring a rightward traverse to the upper snowfield corner). From the ridge notch, Class 2-3 (locally Class 4) scrambling on loose, convoluted sandstone/siltstone slabs, gullies and a short exposed ramp leads to the summit.
overview: The highest of the 'Chief' cluster — Middle Chief (7,120') and Little Big Chief (7,225') sit nearby — Summit Chief anchors the divide between the Waptus and Cooper/Pete Lake country deep in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, on the King-Kittitas county line about 9 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass. Chimney Rock, its line parent, rises immediately southwest across the connecting ridge. First climbed in 1925, it is a big, remote objective reached by one of the longest approaches in the Alpine Lakes: most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a high camp at Vista Lakes rather than a single push.

current.approach: Start at the Pete Lake Trailhead (~2,840 ft) at the end of Cooper Lake Road (Forest Road 46) off the Salmon La Sac Road. Follow the Pete Lake Trail (#1323) roughly 4.5 miles of gentle, mostly flat forest walking along the Cooper River to Pete Lake. From Pete Lake, continue up the Lemah Creek/Lemah Meadows drainage (watch for windfall and thick vine maple in the meadow bypass) to join the Pacific Crest Trail; turn right (north) and climb the PCT's long switchback section roughly 4-4.5 more miles to Lower and Upper Vista Lake (~5,500-5,600 ft) — camp is commonly made here, making this a two-day approach of about 10 miles and 2,800 ft to reach the alpine basin. This is also the last reliable water before the high basin — carry extra, as the route above is reported bone-dry until you're back near Vista Lakes. From Vista Lakes, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country north along Vista Ridge toward Summit Chief Pass, crossing a convoluted series of sandstone/siltstone slabs cut by numerous slots and gullies; stay left (west) of Summit Chief Lake and minimize elevation loss while rounding into the southeast basin below the peak. Many parties stash overnight gear around 6,300 ft in the lower talus basin before the final push. From there, traverse steep hardpan and talus (rockfall potential from parties above) up to a notch near 7,200 ft, then work into the southwest gully system — loose rock and an exposed, slightly outward-dipping slab lead through the final Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. Route-finding through the upper basin and the southwest gully is the crux of the approach; online photos of the south-ridge crossing point are frequently reported as inaccurate, so err toward careful navigation rather than trusting a single beta photo. The route's real crux is often a moat around 7,000 ft where the peak steepens; it can become impassable after mid-July, sometimes earlier in a low-snow year.
approach_variant_names: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved on the standard South Route. Reverse the ascent line exactly: downclimb the loose, exposed southwest gully and its outward-dipping slab back to the ~7,200 ft notch, taking care with the loose rock and steep dirt in the upper 500 feet (this section has real rockfall potential for parties below). Continue down through the talus and hardpan to the 6,300 ft basin (recover any stashed gear here), then retrace the slab traverses back onto Vista Ridge and down to Vista Lakes/the PCT. From Vista Lakes, follow the PCT switchbacks back down to Lemah Meadows and the Pete Lake Trail, then out to the Pete Lake Trailhead. Some parties vary the return by continuing along the PCT to Waptus Lake and crossing Waptus Pass back to the Pete Lake trailhead as an alternate loop. The round trip runs roughly 25 miles car to car, so most parties treat this as an overnight with a basin or Vista Lakes camp rather than a single push.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties, but the exposed, loose Class 3-4 moves near the south-ridge notch and the crux ramp are commonly protected with a light rack and a short rope for less-experienced scramblers; many parties climb it entirely unroped.
rack: Optional light rack (slings) + 30m rope for the crux ramp/notch (used by less-experienced parties)
current.pro_needs: A 30m rope with a small rack of slings/light gear is enough to belay the short crux sections; an ice axe (and traction in early season) is needed for the approach snowfields.
bivy: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
current.rope_note: Published descriptions and trip logs describe the SE Ridge line: talus traverses, loose-rock gullies, and Class 3 rock sections up to a notch near 7,200ft. Standard scramble party travels unroped.

name: East Slopes (Standard)
beta: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, hike the Royal Creek/Upper Dungeness Trail through Royal Basin, continue past Royal Lake into Upper Royal Basin, then leave the maintained trail and travel cross-country to the base of Sundial's east/northeast face. Ascend broken rock and ledges (loose throughout) toward the summit ridge; route-finding is the crux — at least one spot appears to cliff out but a cairned Class 3 crack around the corner allows passage. Continue Class 3 scrambling to the summit.
overview: A minor, seldom-climbed summit in The Needles — a tight cluster of rugged peaks (Mount Clark 7,528 ft, Mount Johnson/Sweat Spire, Mount Walkinshaw, Gilhooley Tower, Gasp Pinnacle) ringing the head of Royal Basin in the far northeastern corner of Olympic National Park, in the Dungeness River drainage above Sequim. It is unrelated to, and nowhere near, the Mount Olympus massif (which lies on the opposite, western side of the range via the Hoh River, a completely separate approach). The peak's name comes from Royal Basin campers watching the morning sun sweep down its east face like a sundial's gnomon shadow. First ascended in 1944 by Adel and William Degenhardt.

current.approach: Drive Hwy 101 to just before Sequim Bay State Park, turn onto Louella Rd, then Palo Alto Rd (becomes FR 28) for about 6 miles, turn right on FR 2880 along the Dungeness River, then in 1.7 miles turn left on FR 2870 and continue roughly 6.5–9 miles (gravel, winds steeply down to a river crossing) to the large Dungeness/Royal Basin trailhead lot (picnic table, vault toilet). Hike the Royal Basin Trail 7.2 miles / 2,500 ft gain to Royal Lake (~5,100 ft), then continue about 1 more mile / 500 ft gain into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600–5,700 ft) below The Needles. From there it's off-trail talus and a gully scramble to Sundial's summit ridge. From Upper Royal Basin, aim for the northeast-facing gully/couloir on climber's right of The Needles group (holds snow into July — axe/crampons helpful); the gully doglegs left below a notch on the summit ridge, then a short, exposed Class 3 scramble leads south to the true summit.
approach_variant_names: Royal Basin to the northeast gully
current.descent: Reverse the northeast couloir and East Face scramble back through Upper Royal Basin to camp at Royal Lake, then retrace the Royal Basin Trail out to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead — this route involves no glacier travel and is unrelated to the Hoh River/Mount Olympus approach.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack required — the standard route is a scramble. No rope or glacier gear is needed on the Royal Basin approach.
current.pro_needs: None for the standard route; a rope and small rack would only come into play on the distinctly harder, separately-named 5.x South Side Face.

name: Superalpine
beta: Starts with an approach pitch of rambly ice leading to a solid ~25 ft near-vertical curtain (WI4), continues up nearly 60m of solid fat WI3 ice in the main gully, eases through 100+m of easier terrain with ice smears through an easy chimney, then finishes with a short WI3 step before the upper snowfields.
overview: A winter ice line up Sloan's west face established in 2020: an approach pitch of rambly ice into a near-vertical curtain, a long main gully of fat WI3 ice, and a short final step before opening onto the upper snowfields.

current.approach: From the Bedal Creek Trailhead (FR 4096), roughly 4-5 hours skinning through the Bedal Creek valley to a 5,000 ft meadow beneath the west face; optionally ascend the ridge to about 5,700 ft and leave skis before the technical climbing.
approach_variant_names: Bedal Creek on skis to the 5,000 ft meadow, then the right-hand line on the west face
current.descent: Either build V-thread rappel anchors and descend the ice line directly, or continue up through the upper snowfields to the Corkscrew Saddle and traverse off via the standard descent to lower terrain.
current.detailed_rack: 6-8 ice screws, optionally a few light rock pieces and a picket.
current.pro_needs: Screw protection through the ice pitches; light rock gear and a picket are optional extras for the upper snow sections.

name: Standard Route (Southwest Face)
beta: Most ascents happen mid-traverse on the Northern Pickets high route (Luna–East Fury–West Fury–Swiss–Spectre Plateau–Phantom–Ghost–Challenger), first strung together as a continuous crest traverse by Wayne Wallace and Josh Kaplan in 2005 (VI 5.7 overall for the traverse, though Swiss itself is comparatively easy 3rd/4th-class terrain). From a camp near West Fury, cross a short glacier/permanent snowfield northwest of West Fury to the Swiss–Fury saddle, then climb the southwest face on notably solid rock (a welcome break from the loose ground nearby) to the summit ridge, descending near the northwest ridge to continue toward Spectre Plateau/Phantom Peak. A separate party approaching from the south (as part of a Mystery Ridge/Northern Pickets enchainment) climbed Swiss's south side directly from a camp at Pickell Pass: straightforward class 3 rock with some ridge-walking needed to identify the true high point, about 2.5 hours round trip. A reliable spring/running water source below the southwest snowfield is a notable resource on an otherwise dry crest.
overview: Swiss Peak has no independently approached line — it is climbed as a link in Picket Range crest traverses. The most-documented ascent gains the West Fury–Swiss col over a small glacier/snowfield, then climbs unusually solid rock up Swiss's southwest face to the broad NW–SE summit ridge; an alternate class 3 line ascends the south side directly from Pickell Pass, and parties approaching from the north describe an 'easy way up' from the Spectre Plateau.

current.approach: Drive WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134). Descend about 1 mile on the Ross Dam trail/service road to Ross Lake, then cross via the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (on-demand, ~$4-5/person) or by hiking/paddling around, and pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake. Follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then continue about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage; leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley (staying on its north side is recommended) to the open basin east of Luna Peak (~4,300 ft) — described as the easiest, least-brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, climb to Access Col, cross to Luna Col, and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss–Fury saddle. An alternate southern approach reaches Swiss via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mt. Crowder's NE ridge down to a camp at Pickell Pass, from which Swiss's south side is climbed directly.
approach_variant_names: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
current.descent: There is no independent 'summit and go home' descent — retreat means reversing whichever approach line was used. From the summit, downclimb near the northwest ridge back toward the saddle with West Fury, re-cross the glacier/snowfield, and either return to a West Fury camp or continue the high traverse. Parties on the southern line downclimb the class 3 south side directly back to the Pickell Pass heather bench camp. Either way, exiting the range afterward requires committing to one of the long approach drainages (Access Creek to Big Beaver Trail/Ross Lake in the north, or Easy Ridge/Chilliwack/Hannegan Pass and Bacon Creek in the south) — both are multi-mile, partly off-trail hikes back to a trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A light glacier/scramble rack is typical rather than a full rock rack: a 30-50m rope for the glacier crossing and any short technical sections, a small rack of cams and nuts for protecting occasional low 5th-class moves on the traverse's harder sections, plus pickets for the snowfield crossing to the West Fury col.
current.pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection needed on Swiss itself given its comparatively solid, moderate-angle rock; gear is carried primarily for the connecting glacier crossings and any exposed 4th/low-5th sections elsewhere on the traverse rather than for Swiss's summit block specifically.
bivy: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Most parties backpack in and camp at Cooney or Martin Lakes rather than attempting the roughly 18-20 mile round trip in a single push. From Cooney Lake, a boot path continues about a mile to gain the broad Southeast Ridge, which is class 1-2 for almost its entire length; only the last few hundred feet below the summit require actual hands-on scrambling over large, mostly stable boulders, with a few exposed class 3 moves right at the top. The peak is frequently linked with Martin Peak via an easy, open class 1-2 ridge walk to the north, forming part of the popular 'Sawtooth Slam' traverse with Mount Bigelow.
overview: Switchback Peak — commonly called Cooney Peak in published descriptions, after Cooney Lake just below its summit — is an 8,300+ ft summit on Sawtooth Ridge in the Methow Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness near the south end of the range above Lake Chelan. Martin Peak (8,375 ft), its nearest higher neighbor, sits 0.96 mi to the north. The summit looks out over Lake Chelan to the west, the Methow Valley to the east, and the Glacier Peak Wilderness to the southwest. West-side drainage feeds Lake Chelan via Prince Creek; east-side drainage feeds the Methow River via Foggy Dew Creek.

current.approach: Two trailheads reach Cooney Lake and the SE Ridge. (1) Foggy Dew Trailhead (end of FR 4340-200, 3,400 ft) — from Twisp, take SR 20 east ~2 mi, then SR 153 south ~12 mi, then Gold Creek Loop Rd/County Rd 1034 and FR 4340 to the FR 4340-200 spur. Hike Foggy Dew Creek Trail #417 about 4.9 miles to its end, then Martin Creek Trail #429 north 2.7 miles and Cooney Lake Trail #434 0.2 mile to Cooney Lake (~7,200 ft); climb to Cooney Pass and the SE Ridge from there. Round trip is roughly 19 miles with about 5,560 ft of gain (a logged trip report took ~5.5 hr up, ~3 hr down). (2) Eagle Lakes/Crater Creek Trailhead (also off FR 4340, 4,700 ft) — follow the Crater Creek/Eagle Lake Trail #431 about 2.5 miles to a signed cutoff heading south toward Martin and Cooney Lakes, then 4.0 miles to Martin Lakes (6,700 ft) and 2.2 more miles to Cooney Lake (7,200 ft) to join the same summit route. The last stretch from the pass to the summit is short but leaves the path for loose rock; the Crater Creek trailhead lot can be full on summer weekend nights (August).
approach_variant_names: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side
current.descent: Reverse the Southeast Ridge down to Cooney Pass and Cooney Lake — the standard line is a walk-down with no rappels. From the lake, retrace to whichever trailhead you started from; parties based at Foggy Dew can vary the return slightly through Merchants Basin.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on this route; it is climbed unroped.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
bivy: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
current.rope_note: Helmet, ice axe and crampons are the kit to carry for the snow sections; no rope is needed for the rock.

name: West Ridge / West Face (via Boiling Lake)
beta: An alternate to the Southeast Ridge standard route: from the Boiling Lake area, a way trail contours below Martin and Switchback Peaks at roughly 7,200-7,300 ft; from there, climbers either pick up a boot path up the west face or climb the west ridge proper (class 2-3) to the summit. It sees far less traffic than the Cooney Lake/Southeast Ridge approach and is more commonly used by parties already in the Boiling Lake/Martin Peak basin as part of a larger Sawtooth Ridge traverse.
overview: A less-traveled alternate line up Switchback's west side, approached via the Boiling Lake basin and the talus benches below Martin Peak, reaching the summit via a boot path on the west face or the class 2-3 west ridge.

current.approach: Reached from the same Crater Creek/Eagle Lakes Trailhead system, branching toward the Boiling Lake basin rather than continuing to Cooney Lake.
current.descent: Reverse the west face/west ridge scramble back to the contour bench and Boiling Lake basin; no rappels reported.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack expected; reportedly unroped scrambling terrain.

name: Table Mountain Trail (Standard)
beta: From the Artist Point parking lot (about 5,075 ft), the Table Mountain Trail climbs a series of tight, exposed switchbacks cut into the mountain's southeast-facing rock face for roughly half a mile and about 400 ft of gain to reach the broad summit plateau. Beyond the switchbacks the trail is gentle, crossing the plateau to tarns with Shuksan views around the 1.3-mile mark; most hikers turn around there. The trail continues west and eventually drops to link with the Chain Lakes Trail system. The route is entirely above treeline, narrow and cliff-edge in its lower half, and not recommended for those uneasy with exposure or for small children; dogs are not allowed.
overview: Table Mountain is a flat-topped andesite lava plateau in the Mount Baker Wilderness, directly above Heather Meadows and the Mt. Baker Ski Area between Mount Baker and Mount Shuksan. From the Artist Point parking lot (~5,100 ft), a short but dramatic trail switchbacks up a basalt/andesite cliff band onto the broad summit plateau, with panoramic views of both Baker and Shuksan. It's one of the most popular short scrambles in the North Cascades, but exposed, sometimes icy switchbacks and an unmarked route beyond the main viewpoint keep it from being a simple stroll.

current.approach: From the Artist Point trailhead (elev. ~5,100 ft, at the end of Mt. Baker Highway/SR 542, GPS approx. 48.847, -121.693) walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot — the signed Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway. The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path that climbs gently before reaching its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there the route ascends a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — this is the crux of the approach: a narrow, exposed catwalk with steep drop-offs toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek drainage 400-800 ft below. Footing here is loose rock and gravel over hard-packed tread, and snow or verglas frequently lingers in this cliff section into July, making it the most hazardous stretch of the whole route; many parties turn back here in early season without traction devices. After roughly 400 ft of gain (about 0.4-0.5 mi from the car) the switchbacks top out on the broad, relatively flat summit plateau ("the table"). From here follow the well-trodden tread west/northwest along the south rim, which gives open views straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail; numerous braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.2 mi you reach the east side of the tabletop with views of Mount Baker and Ptarmigan Ridge, and by 1.3 mi you arrive at two small tarns that frame Mount Shuksan — a natural turnaround for most day hikers and the last easily identified landmark before the trail degrades into a sketchy, unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. There is no reliable water along the route: the summit tarns are shallow, silty, and not worth treating, so carry all water from the car. Overall to the high point is roughly 1.4-1.5 mi one-way with about 700-725 ft of gain from the trailhead.
approach_variant_names: Table Mountain Trail #681 from the Artist Point lot, up the southeast-face switchbacks
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent route — this is a walk-off, out-and-back trail with no rappelling required. From the tarns/plateau area, follow the south-rim tread back east across the tabletop to the head of the switchbacks, then downclimb the same cliff-band switchback trail carved into the southeast face back to the Artist Point parking lot. The switchback section demands the same care going down as coming up (often more, since loose gravel and any residual snow/ice patches are more consequential underfoot on descent, and the exposure is more psychologically apparent facing downhill); microspikes or trekking poles are worth carrying if snow lingers, which is common through early-to-mid summer. Stay on the established tread rather than cutting switchbacks — the rock is loose and the slope drops steeply toward Chain Lakes. No stream crossings or route-finding hazards on the way down beyond staying on the main trail through the braided plateau paths. Total descent is a mirror of the approach: about 1.4-1.5 mi and 700-725 ft back to the car.
current.pro_needs: No rope or rack is needed for the standard route. Some parties use a short handline or simply spot children/nervous hikers through the exposed catwalk sections, but this is not standard practice for competent hikers.
current.rope_note: The trail from Artist Point is a maintained hiking trail with some exposed switchbacks; it is effectively a hike, consistent with the Class 2 rating. No technical gear needed.

name: West Ridge Scramble
beta: From Barclay Lake Trailhead, walk a quarter mile back down the road to a spur road, cross Barclay Creek and climb the Tailgunner Creek drainage/couloir to Tailgunner Pass (~5,320 ft), a broad saddle between Gunn Peak's ridge and Tailgunner. From the pass, scramble up Tailgunner's west ridge and south-facing scree/rock slopes to the summit dome; a narrow summit ledge is the crux and can be exposed or icy if snow lingers. In late-spring snow conditions parties have instead cramponed up a north-slope snow route and surmounted a corniced west-ridge headwall — a more technical, roped variation not represented by the Class 3 rating.
overview: Tailgunner (~5,839 ft, also listed as 5,842 ft on older USGS-derived sources) is a minor summit on the rugged ridge linking Gunn Peak and Wing Peak above Barclay Lake, in the Wild Sky Wilderness of the Skykomish Mountains. Gunn Peak, the range highpoint at 6,244 ft, sits just northwest; Baring Mountain rises across the valley to the south. The peak is trail-less and rarely climbed alone — most parties tag it as a side trip from Gunn Peak or Wing Peak via Tailgunner Pass.

current.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (2,300 ft, ~20-car lot with privy), walk about a quarter mile back down the road to a short spur road and follow it down to Barclay Creek — as of spring 2026 the footlog crossing has been removed for safety with no announced replacement, so expect a rock-hop or ford. Pick up an unmaintained climbers' path up Tailgunner Creek/Tailgunner Ravine; it's brushy with blowdown lower down and passes through a short waterfall ravine before reaching the base of the Tailgunner Couloir. Follow the couloir (steep snow in spring/early summer) to Tailgunner Pass at roughly 5,320-5,400 ft. The round trip is roughly 6-7 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain for Tailgunner alone, and up to about 6,000 ft when Gunn Peak or Wing Peak are combined — budget a long day (8+ hours car-to-car) or plan an overnight camp near the pass.
approach_variant_names: Tailgunner Ravine to Tailgunner Pass
current.descent: Reverse the west ridge back over the gendarmes to the base of the summit block, then descend the same line used on the ascent — either downclimbing (or a short rappel through the crux band in early-season snow/cornice conditions) into the Tailgunner Couloir, or dropping the east slope toward the pass/basin if conditions favor it. A cliff band immediately north of Tailgunner Pass blocks a direct drop from the pass into Gunn Basin, so go around it to the west; carry a rope for the occasional short rappel past the corniced step.
current.detailed_rack: No roped rock climbing is normally required. Some parties carry a rope and a few slings/small rock pieces for extra confidence on the ridge scramble/old cornice remnant, though the standard line is not roped.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection on the standard dry scramble; parties climbing earlier in the season when snow/cornices linger near the summit have carried a rope, a picket, and slings for running belays on the exposed headwall.
current.rope_note: No defined trail; accessed via snow climb on the north slope/west ridge with descent via the east slope. Class 3 scrambling and route-finding; ice axe useful for the snow climb portion, no rope typically carried.

name: North Couloir
beta: Approach via the Honeycomb Glacier — either descending from a high camp on Kololo Peaks or traversing in from the White River side over the PCT/Whitechuck and Suiattle Glaciers — to a col west of Tenpeak, then cross onto the Honeycomb Glacier and traverse to the couloir's base. Climb the roughly 1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree couloir (crampons and ice axe, or ski crampons for splitboard/ski parties), then scramble to the NW Ridge where one 5.4 rock pitch leads to the summit.
overview: A prominent snow/ski couloir splitting Tenpeak's north face, reached by traversing in from the Honeycomb Glacier; a sustained ~35-degree, roughly 1,200-ft snow climb finishes with one short 5.4 rock pitch to the summit via the NW Ridge.

current.approach: From the White River Trailhead (see Southeast Route access), reach the upper Whitechuck/Suiattle Glacier basin via the PCT and cross to the Honeycomb Glacier, or descend the Honeycomb Glacier northward from a high camp on Kololo Peaks (8,220 ft) further west along the Glacier Peak massif. Traverse the glacier to the col just west of Tenpeak and the base of the north couloir.
approach_variant_names: Over the col west of Tenpeak and down the Honeycomb Glacier to the couloir's base
current.descent: From the summit, reverse the short 5.4 pitch back to the top of the couloir. Ski parties descend the couloir itself (firm corn snow in the morning softening through the day); climbers on foot downclimb the ~1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree snow to the Honeycomb Glacier and retrace the approach.
current.detailed_rack: A few pieces of rock protection (small nuts/cams) and a rope sufficient for one short 5.4 pitch near the summit; add a standard glacier travel kit (rope, crevasse-rescue hardware) if approaching via the Honeycomb/Suiattle Glaciers.
current.pro_needs: Minimal — a light rock rack for one short pitch, plus glacier travel protection on the approach.
bivy: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River

name: Southeast Route / Standard
beta: From Thunder Basin at 5,180 feet, ascend snowfields and rocky slopes toward the summit block. The final two pitches involve Class 4 scrambling up a gully left of the summit col (approximately 85 feet to a ledge), followed by a longer pitch up a face toward a broken chimney containing a good jam crack that leads directly to the summit. Crampons and ice axe essential for snowfield sections. A fixed pin exists for rappel descent assistance. The route sees minimal traffic and requires solid route-finding skills.
overview: Tenpeak Mountain is a rugged, partly glaciated 8,312' summit in the Dakobed Range, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness southeast of Glacier Peak itself. Cretaceous-age granitic rock, small hanging glaciers on its flanks, and a 4,200-ft north face dropping to the Suiattle Valley give it real alpine character despite its modest elevation. First ascended September 21, 1940 by Lloyd Anderson and Tom Campbell via essentially this same Southeast Slope line. It is a low-traffic objective — most parties reach it via a long, largely cross-country approach from the White River Trailhead near Lake Wenatchee (Chelan County side) or, less commonly, from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead off the Mountain Loop Highway (Snohomish County side).

current.approach: Primary approach (White River side): From Hwy 2 at Coles Corner, follow Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (Forest Road 6400) to its end at the White River/Indian Creek Trailhead (~2,300 ft). Hike the White River Trail #1507 about 6 miles to the Thunder Creek crossing. A half mile past Thunder Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up an old, unmaintained sheep trail that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage through avalanche debris and brush to a lower basin (~4,175 ft), then steeply up to the upper Thunder Basin (~5,180 ft, about 9 miles and 2,900 ft above the trailhead) — the standard high camp with a direct view of Tenpeak. Alternate approach (North Fork Sauk / west side): drive the Mountain Loop Highway to Forest Road 49 and the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,100 ft), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country via Boulder Pass and the Napeequa Valley to Tenpeak's north/northeast side — a much longer, more committing option (reported as ~31 miles and 13,500 ft of gain over 3 days for a full traverse) with 20+ stream crossings and dense brush. From the Thunder Basin camp, the route continues across talus and snow to a col east of the summit block (ice axe/crampons typically needed for the sometimes-firm snow), then climbs a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system, followed by a broken chimney/face pitch (Class 4 to easy Class 5 depending on conditions) to the summit; rock in the gully and chimney is loose, so helmet up and manage rope/party spacing to avoid dropping rock on others below. Above a camp at about 4,200 ft by Thunder Creek, dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 ft is the hardest bushwhacking before Thunder Basin opens up.
approach_variant_names: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
North Fork Sauk Trail, the PCT and Boulder Pass from the west
current.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb (or rappel, if wet/loose) the broken chimney/face and gully back to the col, then descend the snow/talus back into Thunder Basin. From Thunder Basin, retrace the sheep trail down to the White River Trail junction and hike out to the trailhead. There are no fixed anchors reported on the gully/chimney — parties needing to rappel use natural anchors (horns, chockstones) and should carry extra webbing/cord.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit plus a few small pieces and slings for the exposed Class 4 summit step.
current.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel and steep snow lead to an exposed Class 4 summit block; minimal rock pro needed.

name: South Couloir (Standard Route)
beta: A long, mostly non-technical mountaineering route that is more of a route-finding and stamina challenge than a climbing one. From the Lena Lake Trailhead, hike past Lena Lake and through the Valley of the Silent Men to a base-camp area near where the trail meets Lena Creek's forks. From there, climbers' paths lead up the creek drainage to a broad avalanche slope/meadow below the first cliff band; cross this and enter the couloir (snow- or rock-filled depending on season), following it up through the narrow "Hourglass" constriction near ~5,800 ft. Above the Hourglass the couloir broadens; work up and right, staying on firmer rock, then trend back left/up through loose scree to the summit. Early/mid-season the couloir holds continuous snow (ice axe and crampons required, with snow up to 40-45 degrees); by late summer it is a loose, snow-free scree-and-rock scramble.
overview: The standard and most-climbed route up The Brothers' higher south summit (Mt. Edward, ~6,868'), one of the most recognizable peaks on the Seattle skyline. From the Lena Lake/Brothers trailhead it's about 8.5 miles and 6,100+ ft one-way (roughly 17 miles round trip): 3 miles on the maintained Lena Lake Trail #810 to Lower Lena Lake, then 2.8 miles on the rougher Brothers Trail #821 up the East Fork Lena Creek through the narrow, cliff-walled Valley of the Silent Men to campsites around 2,900-3,000'. From camp the route follows an old avalanche path into the South Couloir, exits it to the west onto scree around 5,000', makes an ascending rightward traverse below cliffs to the Hourglass — a narrow class 3-4 notch around 5,800' that is the technical crux — then climbs loose scree/talus to the summit ridge. Early in the season (roughly April-June) the couloir and Hourglass hold snow and the route climbs more like a moderate PD snow route (axe/crampons); by late summer the snow melts out and the same terrain becomes a looser, more exposed class 3-4 scramble with real rockfall hazard, especially with other parties climbing above.

current.approach: From the Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25 at roughly 700 ft, hike the maintained Lena Lake Trail about 3 miles and ~1,100 ft of gain through second-growth and old-growth forest, crossing several creek drainages on the way, to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft) — a popular backpacking destination with a ranger station and established campsites, and the last easy, reliable water/camping before the climbers' route. Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Brothers Trail' boot path, which continues up the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth 'Valley of the Silent Men' for roughly another 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp (sometimes called Camp Brothers) at about 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring — most parties treat this as their high camp for a two-day ascent. From camp, leave the tread and follow a climbers' path along the west fork of Lena Creek for about a mile; this crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs (some with hand-lines/notches cut in) obscure the route and creek fords may be required — go carefully, especially with a full pack. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs to the base of the South Couloir around 4,000-4,300 ft. Ascend the couloir (firm snow in early season, loose scree by mid/late summer) a few hundred feet, then exit onto its west side and continue up scree to about 5,000 ft, making an ascending rightward traverse below cliff bands to reach the crest of a semi-open spur. From the spur, work up and right to the base of 'the Hourglass,' a narrow rock/snow constriction that is the technical crux of the approach to the summit block (Class 3 scrambling, or a steep 35-45° snow climb in early season requiring an axe and solid self-arrest skills — watch for a moat opening at its base as the snow recedes). Above the Hourglass, continue on scree or snow toward the summit ridge and watch closely for a cairned, easy-to-miss notch on the right (climbers describe it as a 'dwarf door' — nearly invisible until you're directly in front of it); this notch is the route-finding key to the final gully leading to the true south summit, the last roughly 200 vertical feet of which is Class 4 with real exposure. Water is reliable at Lena Lake and along Lena Creek up to high camp; above camp, plan on snowmelt or carrying water, as there's nothing reliable once you're on the scree/couloir.
approach_variant_names: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
Early-season snow ascent
current.descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line exactly, and for most parties it is a downclimb with no rappelling: down-climb the exposed Class 4 summit block back through the cairned notch (some parties belay or place a single short rappel of roughly 30-50 ft here off a sling around a rock horn or chockstone if the party is inexperienced, the rock is wet, or exposure has anyone spooked — there is no fixed/bolted rappel station reported, so bring a sling/cord and be prepared to build a natural anchor if you want the extra protection), then continue down through the Hourglass with careful, deliberate downclimbing on loose Class 3 rock (this is the section most prone to kicking rockfall onto anyone below, so descend one at a time with the party grouped tightly or well spread out). Below the Hourglass, downclimb or plunge-step/glissade the scree and snow of the South Couloir back to treeline (glissading is common on lingering snow but watch for a runout onto rock or the moat near the couloir's base), then pick up the climbers' path back through the avalanche debris/slide-alder crossing, through the Valley of the Silent Men, past high camp, and back down the Brothers Trail and Lena Lake Trail to the trailhead. Overall this route has no mandatory technical rappels — it is a walk-off/downclimb — but treat the summit-block notch as an optional single-rappel section if conditions or party experience warrant it. Descent hazards include loose, exposure-prone downclimbing at the notch and through the Hourglass, rockfall onto lower party members, softening/isothermal snow in the couloir on warm afternoons (raising wet-slide and post-holing risk), and simple fatigue-driven route-finding errors re-locating the 'dwarf door' notch and the correct exit from the couloir on the way down — several trip reports flag the descent as the part where parties get off-route, not the ascent.
current.detailed_rack: No rock rack needed for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: None typical for the standard line; a rope is optional for less experienced parties on the upper steps
bivy: Brothers base camp at Lena Forks
current.rope_note: Standard basic climb: steep snow couloir requiring ice axe/crampons in early/winter/late season; can become a snow-free 3rd-class scramble by late August. Trip reports show a rope is sometimes rigged as a handline (with prusiks) on sustained ~30-degree snow above 'The Hourglass' where moats form on both sides.

name: Brothers Traverse (North Peak to South Peak)
beta: Fourth-class scrambling leads to a notch near 6,100 ft and a descent on steep snow into the Great Basin, below the North Brother. From there the traverse is 7 roped pitches (statically belayed, though simulclimbing is possible): moderate snow pitches on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed rock-and-snow sections with moat belays, and a final steep couloir ascent to the South Brother summit. The route is recommended north-to-south.
overview: A committing ridge traverse linking The Brothers' North and South summits, mixing fourth-class scrambling, moderate snow pitches through the 'Great Basin,' and a sparsely protected rock traverse before finishing up a couloir to the South Brother summit.

current.approach: Follow the same Lena Lake / Brothers Trail approach used for the South Couloir to established climbers' camp (~6 miles from the trailhead), then cross the creek westward, cross a slide meadow and old burn scar, and climb a wide gully north to about 5,500 ft to gain the North Peak side of the mountain.
approach_variant_names: Lena Lake Trail and the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp, then the North Peak side
current.descent: From the South Brother summit, descend the South Brother's standard route rather than reversing the ridge traverse: go down the east-facing gully to the 5,500 ft base camp area, then retrace the trail descent to Lena Lake Trailhead (additional 4-5 hours).
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack plus snow pickets.
rack: A handful of slings for rock/rappel anchors
current.pro_needs: Protection is sparse on parts of the rock traverse; snow pickets are needed for the moderate snow pitches and moat belays.
bivy: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
current.rope_note: Committing traverse between the two summits combining moderate snow pitches (pickets + rock gear for pro) with a sparsely-protected rock traverse. Teams of 2-3 reportedly use a 30m glacier-style rope with one picket each; some experienced parties climb it as 7 statically-belayed pitches. Best done early season (April-May) before brush fills the approach gullies.

name: The Cave Route
beta: Starts on the north side of the tower, about 50 feet below the notch, at two semi-parallel diagonal cracks that form the crux. After the diagonals, the route follows a flake past a dead tree to a belay tree (reportedly deteriorating — back it up with gear). Pitch 2 traverses left beneath an overhang to a corner, then continues about 20 feet to the mouth of a cave, which is climbed through (~20 feet) to a belay on the far side. Pitch 3 climbs an easier crack and face to a tree belay at the summit.
overview: A serious, rarely repeated line on Concord's north side, climbed in three pitches of highly variable rock — described by the route's documenter as ranging from crumbly ('oatmeal') rock and scree to sound slabs with one good crack. The route is generally not recommended except for parties very solid at the grade.

current.approach: Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), ~30 miles west of Winthrop, ~1 mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass required. Hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climber's boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs/talus/meadow to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (often snow-filled and icy into late June, high rockfall risk after snowmelt). From the notch, drop about 50 feet down the gully on the north side of Concord Tower to the start of the two diagonal cracks that mark the route.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then drop 50 feet down the north side
current.descent: Rappel off the summit's west side, stopping at the mid-height station if you carry a single 60 m rope, to a ledge; move right along it and make one more rappel down the north face to the notch.
current.detailed_rack: A standard trad rack up to 4 inches, plus extra slings/alpine draws to manage drag on the traversing second pitch.
rack: Extra slings/alpine draws (6) for the traversing P2
current.pro_needs: Marginal to nonexistent protection at the crux highstep; not a route to rely on gear.
current.rope_note: 3 pitches (P1 crux diagonal cracks, P2 exposed leftward traverse through/around 'the cave', P3 5.4 crack to face climbing). The 'R' rating comes from the poorly protected P1 crux; on the traversing P2, place directional gear to protect the second.

name: Southeast Face
beta: From the high camp, traverse beneath the steep east face to the southeast side of the peak, where a hidden gully gives easy access to the face. Climb a chimney about 200 ft high, then a slabby face. Below the summit slab there are a few harder moves where the route mixes face and ridge climbing, with some scrubby vegetation. Allow about three hours from timberline. Because the Pickets guard several summits from a shared basin, parties often combine this peak with Mount Degenhardt, Mount Terror, or Inspiration Peak on the same trip.
overview: Officially "Pinnacle Peak" on USGS maps, but almost universally called The Chopping Block for its distinctive squarish, blocky summit block. It sits at the south end of the Barrier Ridge in the Southern Pickets, North Cascades National Park, dividing Terror Creek Basin from Crescent Creek Basin, and is visible from the Newhalem visitor center on clear days. First climbed in 1932 by Bill Degenhardt and H. V. Strandberg — their summit cairn reportedly remained undisturbed for decades — it's now a common secondary objective for parties in the Southern Pickets for Mount Terror, Mount Degenhardt, or the Twin Needles.

current.approach: Drive SR 20 to Newhalem, which is reachable year-round from the west (Marblemount/Concrete) since the seasonal highway closure gate sits farther east near Ross Dam/Diablo. Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead on the north side of SR 20, across from Newhalem Campground (take the left just past crossing Goodell Creek, past the gravel pit, to road's end by the creek). Hike the old Goodell Creek Trail — a former logging-road bed — roughly 4 miles up-valley to the Terror Creek Trail junction, marked by a large cairn. About a mile beyond, at around 2,000 ft, cross Terror Creek on a log or by wading (calf-deep by late summer; the last reliable water before high camp), then climb one of the steepest maintained climbers' trails in the Cascades, gaining the ridge crest between Terror and Crescent Creeks via roots and 3rd-class dirt scrambling. Once on the crest — brushy with blueberry bushes and prone to fading in and out — follow it northwest several miles toward Stump Hollow (~5,600 ft) or the Chopping Block/Barrier Ridge camps overlooking Crescent Creek Basin and Mount Terror. Most parties reach camp in one long, steep day and climb the peak the next. Total approach is roughly 6-7 miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain to camp.
current.descent: Descend the face by about seven low-angle rappels, watching for loose rock. Parties combining the Chopping Block with Mount Degenhardt or the Twin Needles typically continue along the Barrier/Chopping Block Ridge rather than dropping straight back to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack is enough: a 200-ft chimney and a slabby face, low fifth class at most. A small set of nuts and cams plus slings covers belays on the exposed sections, and the descent needs gear for about seven rappels.
current.pro_needs: A light alpine rack for the chimney and the slab, plus slings and cord for about seven rappels on the descent.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
current.rope_note: Low-fifth-class alpine rock route (5.5, Grade II): a 200-ft chimney and a slabby face, reached by a hidden gully on the southeast side. A light rack covers it; the descent is about seven low-angle rappels.

name: The Devils Club
beta: Fred Beckey reportedly attempted this face earlier and found it traumatic enough to never return, and it came to be regarded as a last great problem perhaps best left unclimbed. Layton and Wolfe finally forced a route in 2005 after a brutal approach, climbing banded gneiss that offered very little solid protection; every hold reportedly required testing, and pitons often wouldn't set. Note: the grade/length is variously given as V+ 5.9+ A2- and ~2,500 ft, and as V+ 5.11- and 2,400 ft — the latter figures are used here, but treat the discrepancy as a sign of how approximate any grade is on this kind of loose, unrepeated wall.
overview: The Devils Club is a serious, remote Grade V alpine rock route up the roughly 2,000-2,500 ft east face of Southeast Mox Peak ("Hard Mox"), one of the most committing big walls in the Lower 48 given its approach. First climbed by Mike Layton and Eric (Erik) Wolfe over August 31-September 1, 2005, with one bivouac partway up the wall. Notably, the FA party topped out the East Face but — out of food and water — did not continue on to Southeast Mox's true summit; parties repeating the route should clarify whether their objective is the wall itself or the actual summit (which would require additional scrambling/climbing beyond the top of the face). A second-ascent party (Eric Wehrly, 2008) climbed a variation.

current.approach: Access starts on Ross Lake: from the Ross Dam trailhead on SR-20 (near milepost 134), hike the short Ross Dam Trail down to Ross Lake Resort, then take the resort's water taxi (or paddle a canoe) about 15 miles up-lake to the Little Beaver Creek dock. From the dock, follow the maintained (but lightly traveled) Little Beaver Trail west, paralleling Little Beaver Creek through cedar-fir forest with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, about 4.6-5 miles to Perry Creek Camp/Shelter, a three-sided log shelter that marks the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward the Mox massif. From Perry Creek Camp there is no trail: the standard line follows the Perry Creek drainage south, and staying in or right beside the creekbed itself gives the fastest travel (easy rock-hopping and scrambling) up to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the creek and forces climbers up onto a bank. The south (true left) side of the drainage is preferred here — it holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths, while the north side is a nearly impenetrable slide-alder thicket. Above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber where travel speed improves to roughly 2-3 mph, eventually gaining the upper Perry Creek/Mox basin cirque below the connecting ridge to Southeast Mox, with talus and (season-dependent) snowfields and moats guarding the final approach to the toe of the 2,400-2,500 ft East Face. This is a genuinely serious approach, not a formality: the FA party (Layton/Wolfe, 2005) needed two full days in the rain from the lake to the base — 4.5 miles of trail, then roughly 14 hours of brush and creek travel up Perry Creek — and described it as one of the worst approaches in the Cascades. Expect cold creek fords, soaked gear, torn-up skin from devil's club and slide alder (the plant the route is named for), and real route-finding judgment calls about which side of the drainage to commit to. Water is abundant the entire way (Little Beaver Creek, Perry Creek) but should be treated.
approach_variant_names: Ross Lake to the Little Beaver landing, then the Perry Creek drainage
current.descent: The East Face is rappelled top to bottom on its own line — there is no walk-off, and no fixed/bolted rappel stations exist anywhere on the route; every anchor is natural (slung horns, chockstones/gear anchors) built on the spot, so a party needs full natural-anchor-building skill and a rack sufficient to leave gear behind. The FA party (Layton/Wolfe) rappelled the entire 2,400-2,500 ft face using two ropes tied together to maximize each rappel's reach, angling the line closer to the northeast ridge than their ascent line, especially on the lower half, to find sounder anchor rock and avoid the loosest terrain in the direct fall line. Their first rappel hung up and forced a strenuous full return to the top to free it before they could continue; from there, roughly a dozen more rappels (about 13 total) got them to the ground, finishing around 3:30 a.m. after an 18-hour continuous push from the base. At the bottom they waded back across the creek chest-deep rather than re-entering the alder/devil's club to reach their tent. Later parties should plan on a similar count (very roughly a dozen-plus rappels with a doubled/joined-rope setup) but treat that as an estimate scaled from a single documented descent, not a fixed number — anchor placement is judgment-call and can shift the rappel line and count. Expect loose, sometimes rotten rock the entire way (a defining hazard of the route), real risk of stuck ropes given the wandering natural-anchor line, and likely a night finish if the climb runs long, so headlamps and a plan for rope work in the dark should be assumed.
current.detailed_rack: The first-ascent account does not specify an exact rack; expect to carry a broad trad selection plus thin gear (small cams/wires, and pitons if you carry them), since the party reported protection was sparse throughout and pitons frequently would not set in the loose rock.
rack: A few pitons (optional, for old/thin placements)
Significant extra cord/webbing for gear rap anchors (no bolts on route)
current.pro_needs: Protection was reported as marginal to absent for long stretches — this is an R/X route regardless of the exact grade cited; a big, varied rack won't compensate for the rock quality.
current.rope_note: Southeast Mox Peak, 2,500ft East Face big-wall alpine route (25 pitches). First ascent placed no bolts and rappelled the route entirely on gear anchors, extremely remote/serious. Full trad rack plus abundant rap-anchor cord essential.

name: The Exorcism of Mark Hanna
beta: Pitch 2 holds two distinct cruxes and can be French-freed at 5.10a for parties not wanting to commit to the full 5.11a; slab sections give way to steep, balancy overlap moves. A belay bolt marks the route's start on a small ledge.
overview: A shorter, 3-pitch 5.11a trad route on M&M Wall reached via the Supercave approach gully; a quicker outing than the wall's big multi-pitch free lines.

current.approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns (and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit). From the highway, head directly uphill toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
approach_variant_names: Supercave gully to the lower ledge
current.descent: The route is bolted for rappelling and is designed to be descended on its own line with one 70 m rope. From the top anchors, rappel back down to the belay bolt on the small ledge at the base of the apron. The route runs almost directly below Ellen Pea, so that line can serve as an alternative way up or down. From the base, scramble down the Supercave gully, the reverse of the approach, to the pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20.
current.detailed_rack: A standard trad rack up to 1 inch, plus quickdraws and runners; a mix of bolts and gear protects the two pitch-2 cruxes.
current.pro_needs: Mixed bolt-and-gear protection; standard rack to 1 inch covers the route, with bolts backing up the crux moves on pitch 2.
bivy: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout

name: The Hitchhiker
beta: Ascends the south face starting in a small left-facing bolted dihedral; a highlight is a 5.11- slab traverse around pitch 5. Rated 3.8/5 by climbers with 182+ votes, considered a quality alpine trad testpiece alongside the neighboring Passenger and South Arete.
overview: A long, sustained mixed free/bolted line up the steep southeast face of SEWS, starting about 100 ft right of The Passenger. Established over three visits between July and September 2007 by Bryan Burdo and Scott Johnston.

current.approach: Approach as for the Passenger: Blue Lake Trailhead climber's trail (~1 hour) to the South Arete base, then traverse down and right along the base of the wall past the Passenger's fir-tree/double-crack start, continuing roughly another 100 ft to a small left-facing dihedral with 4 bolts — the Hitchhiker's start, on the steep SE face of the spire.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then past the Passenger's fir tree another hundred feet to the four-bolt dihedral
current.descent: The Hitchhiker is a long day (up to 8 hours for 9 pitches) of sustained face climbing with about 20 bolts but still requiring a full trad rack; it tops out at the summit rather than being descended via its own rappel line. From the top, take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete (3rd/4th class with a short, more exposed step) to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is standard and matches the rope length noted in the route's protection beta) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base, then hike out via the climber's trail to Blue Lake Trail.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles of cams up to 2 inches plus a standard set of nuts; a 60m rope is used for the route and rappels.
current.pro_needs: Well-bolted on the technical pitches (about 20 bolts total) but still needs a full trad rack for the crack sections.
current.rope_note: 9-pitch 5.11- SEWS route; standard hard-free alpine rack, similar to Southern Man on the same wall.

name: Sawtooth Range Scramble
beta: Above Flapjack Lakes, the standard approach leaves the Gladys Divide trail at about 4,400 ft, short of the divide near a small pond, and climbs an open snow/rock slope southeast toward Sawtooth Pass - snow lingers on it into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. Below the pass, traverse right on loose, exposed class 3-4 ground under the west face of The Fin to the notch south of The Horn. Do not underestimate The Horn as a simple scramble: despite the modest 5.5 grade, the final summit pitch is run-out and the rock demands careful gear placement.
overview: The Horn is a rugged basalt pinnacle on Sawtooth Ridge, in the far southeastern corner of Olympic National Park on the crest between Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln — east of Flapjack Lakes, not in the Lake of the Angels/Putvin drainage to the north (a different part of the southeastern Olympics). It shares its approach (Staircase, Flapjack Lakes, Gladys Divide) with Mount Cruiser and The Fin. Though it has been called a Class 3-4 scramble, parties agree it is a genuine roped 5th-class trad route (5.5, R) on some of the best pillow basalt the Olympic Range has to offer, with real exposure and sparse protection.

current.approach: Drive Hwy 101 to Hoodsport, then SR-119 (North Lake Cushman Road, becomes FR-24 past the lake) roughly 9 miles to the Staircase Ranger Station/trailhead (~800 ft) in the SE corner of Olympic National Park. Hike the North Fork Skokomish River Trail ~3.4 miles to the Spike Camp junction, then climb steeply another ~3.6 miles to Flapjack Lakes (~4,000 ft, 8 miles from the trailhead) — a limited-entry wilderness camping zone, so reserve a permit well ahead. From Flapjack Lakes, follow the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400 ft, then leave it and climb cross-country southeast toward Sawtooth Pass to reach the base of The Fin and The Horn. Round-trip approach mileage to Gladys Divide alone runs close to 19 miles with roughly 4,000+ ft of net gain, before the additional ridge travel and the climb itself — this is realistically a backpack-in with a high camp, not a day trip from the road.
approach_variant_names: Sawtooth crest traverse under The Fin's west face
current.descent: Descend by rappelling from the summit notch — carrying two ropes allows a full double-rope rappel back down to the notch south of The Horn — then reverse the scramble under The Fin's west face to regain the ridge. Parties completing the fuller Sawtooth Ridge traverse have described the eventual descent off the ridge system as a brushy, slow 'controlled fall' through slide alder and devil's club; expect the broader cross-country return to Flapjack Lakes/Gladys Divide to be vegetated and time-consuming regardless of exact line.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack (small-to-medium nuts and cams) covers the short technical pitch at The Horn's notch; long slings help manage rope drag on the wandering line.
rack: Small-to-medium rack, doubles in finger-to-hand sizes (to 3")
A few small pitons and tat for aging anchors
Two ropes for a double-rope rappel off the summit notch
current.pro_needs: Rack to 3in; both the SE and SW routes are R-rated (runout/sparsely protected), so plan on a mix of small-to-medium cams/nuts plus a few pitons and tat for anchors — this is not a well-protected or bolted route.
bivy: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
current.rope_note: SE/SW routes off the notch south of The Horn, both rated 5.5 trad on pillow basalt; the 'R' rating implies sparser protection than typical, so extra small-to-medium gear for building solid placements is worth carrying.

name: The L & H Route (Free Variation)
