beta: Shares its start with The Tiger before splitting into its own line. Quality 5.10 climbing (some sections still lichen-flecked) is interspersed with harder cruxes on immaculate rock; treat the grades as provisional, since the route has seen very few repeats. The original 1969 aid ascent was protected almost entirely by pitons, plus 1 bolt; the free ascent added 3 protection bolts (with FA-party Jim Langdon's permission) on sections that had been aided via upward-driven knifeblade pitons.
overview: The free version of the 1969 Langdon-Hargis aid line up M&M Wall, freed in 2015 by Blake Herrington and Max Tepfer; an 8-pitch outing on immaculate granite with a sustained 5.12 crux pitch widely regarded as one of the best pitches of 5.12 on granite anywhere in the state.

current.approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns (and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit). From the highway, head directly uphill toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
approach_variant_names: Supercave gully to the shared start at the foot of the wall
current.descent: From the top, rappel down the Ellen Pea line using two ropes (diagonal rappelling is required in places), or walk down via the 3rd-class terrain to the west.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack to #3 (BD size), with triples of the smaller cam sizes (purple C3 through 0.5"), doubles of 0.75" and 1", plus a standard set of stoppers and RPs. Three protection bolts and three anchor bolts were added on the free ascent with the original first-ascensionist's permission.
current.pro_needs: A gear-intensive free line: small cams triple-racked for sustained thin sections, supplemented by a handful of fixed bolts on the hardest crux moves; several older fixed pitons remain from the original 1969 aid ascent and should not be trusted.
bivy: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout

name: The Meeperland Empire
beta: A crux start on below-average rock quality for Keechelus, then the route is basically over. Also toprope-able by walking up, but the anchor ledge is slanting and dirty — use a personal anchor system (PAS) when clipping in.
overview: A short, crux-loaded route below all the other East Face lines, directly beneath Glacier View Temple.

current.approach: From Nocturnal Pulse, descend about 200 ft into the talus field; the anchor becomes visible before reaching the route itself.
current.descent: Lower from the chain anchor; the anchor ledge is slanting and dirty, so clip in with a PAS before unroping or transitioning.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 3 bolts to a chain anchor on a slanting, dirty ledge.
current.pro_needs: Short sport rack of 3 quickdraws; bring a PAS for the anchor transition.

name: Neve Glacier Approach / Standard
beta: Follow the standard Snowfield Peak approach via Pyramid Lake to reach the Colonial-Neve col (approximately 6,800-6,900 feet). Traverse westward along the Neve Glacier staying near the glacier edge to avoid steep snow. Pass Horseman's Pack (8,156 ft) and The Horseman (7,760 ft), then turn north following the glacier edge to the southeast ridge of The Needle. Ascend the snow arete, bypassing the bergshrund, to gain the rocky ridge. Climb sustained Class 3 scrambling with full exposure, turning west around a corner. The final knife-edge ridge section before the summit can be crossed straddled (à cheval) or via an awkward mantle traverse. Exposed moves throughout.
overview: A minor rock horn on the far western rim of the Neve Glacier icecap in North Cascades National Park, about a mile northwest of Snowfield Peak (USGS maps mislabel it immediately west of Snowfield). First climbed August 1, 1931 by William A. Degenhardt and Herbert V. Strandberg — the same party that first summited Snowfield Peak. With only ~305 ft of prominence it is almost always climbed as a bonus summit tacked onto a Snowfield Peak or Colonial/Neve glacier circuit rather than as a stand-alone objective.

current.approach: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead (an unmarked gravel pullout on the north shoulder of WA-20, about 21 mi east of Marblemount and just west of Diablo Dam), follow the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail 2.1 mi and roughly 1,500 ft to Pyramid Lake. Pick up the unmaintained climbers' path around the right (east) side of the lake; it climbs steep, root-laced forest for about 2,000 ft before opening into heather and boulder terrain, then follows a narrowing ridge and a scree/boulder traverse (snow-covered into midsummer) to the toe of the Colonial Glacier. Most parties camp on the flat bench at about 6,100 ft below the glacier (backcountry permit required). From camp, rope up and travel south up the Colonial Glacier to a col at about 6,900 ft, drop about 200 ft onto the Neve Glacier icecap, and cross toward Snowfield Peak before diverting west along the glacier rim to The Needle's southeast ridge as described in the route beta.
approach_variant_names: Colonial Glacier col to the Neve rim
current.descent: Rappel about 25 ft off the large summit flake down the north face to a ledge, walk back to the ledge below the gendarme, and reverse the ridge to the glacier rim, re-cross the Neve and Colonial Glaciers (crevasse bridges will typically be softer and wider than on the morning crossing), regain the roughly 6,900 ft col, and descend to camp. From camp, retrace the climbers' trail and Pyramid Lake Trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit plus a few small pieces and slings for the short exposed summit rock.
current.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel followed by a short exposed Class 4 scramble; minimal rock protection needed.

name: The Perfect Crime (with variations...)
beta: A 'choose-your-own-adventure' wall route: the topo describes a default line but notes several parallel options at P1, P3 and P4. Rock is generally solid but still lichen-covered and loose in spots since the routes are relatively young (established 2007+). No bolts and very little fixed gear - tree slings mark some anchors, including a memorable 'spiral tree' landmark on P3.
overview: A 5-pitch (6 counting the short P2.5 link), 800-ft moderate trad line up the right side of Cutthroat Wall, weaving through featured granite - corners, cracks and an easy alpine slab finish past a distinctive spiral tree - with multiple variations at nearly every pitch.

current.approach: This is a distinct approach from the one used for Cutthroat Peak, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass with no maintained trail. For Cutthroat Wall, start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail #483 from the Cutthroat Trailhead kiosk. After a short distance on the main trail, leave it via a cairned path that cuts into the forest, then follow cairns and a climbers' path (roughly 1.5-2 miles, 45 min-2 hrs total) through brush and talus, trending toward the buttress, to reach the base of Cutthroat Wall.
approach_variant_names: Cutthroat Creek trail #483 from the Cutthroat Lake trailhead
current.descent: From the topout, walk roughly 100-200 ft along the ridge/east to a minor notch separating the westernmost buttress from the higher central buttress, marked by a slung horn/tree. A single-rope rappel (over a chockstone tunnel that can snag the rope on the pull) drops to a dirty ramp with a small cave. From there, find and follow an upward-trending gully or ledge system on skier's left (do NOT descend directly down the obvious gully below the notch, which is loose and hazardous), curving around back to grassy terrain near the base of the routes. Use a single 70m rope.
current.detailed_rack: Standard Washington Pass rack: stoppers, small cams, a double set of cams up to big hand size, and a single fist-sized piece. Minimal fixed gear beyond occasional tree slings; a single 70m rope is recommended over doubles.
current.pro_needs: Stoppers plus a doubled cam rack from small through hand size and one fist-sized piece; natural anchors (trees, horns) are used at several belays and the rap station.
bivy: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

name: East Ridge
beta: Known only from Wayne Wallace, Colin Haley (age 17), and Mark Bunker's four-day, 14-summit Southern Pickets Enchainment (July 2003), where Pyramid was climbed via its east ridge/face at II 5.8 immediately after Inspiration Peak and before Mt. Degenhardt. It is not established as a stand-alone objective, so no dedicated approach or descent for climbing this line on its own is known — parties would likely use the same general approach as the South Route (Terror Basin/Crescent Creek Basin via the Barrier crossing), but that connection is an assumption, not confirmed.
overview: The technical line up Pyramid's east side, climbed as the 5th of 14 summits during the first complete Southern Pickets Enchainment; rated II 5.8, with rock the first party found 'surprisingly beautiful' despite the peak's chossy reputation.

name: South Route
beta: From a high camp near the Terror Glacier or in Crescent Creek Basin, parties cross The Barrier (the connecting ridge between Terror and Crescent Creek basins) and work across broken, sometimes loose terrain toward the notch south of Mount Degenhardt, then traverse east along the connecting ridge onto Pyramid's west side. The line climbs a gully/couloir system on scrambling terrain with a few low fifth-class moves; staying left in the gully rather than attempting the overhanging rock directly above it is reported as the easier, more sensible line. Rock quality is inconsistent — solid gneiss in places, dirt- and choss-covered in others — and the peak sees comparatively little independent traffic, most parties tagging it en route between Degenhardt and Inspiration Peak.
overview: The Pyramid is a compact, seldom-visited summit on the crest of the Southern Pickets, set on the ridge between Mount Degenhardt to the west and Inspiration Peak to the east. At roughly 7,920 ft it is the shortest of the range's named summits, overshadowed by its 8,000-ft-plus neighbors, and is almost never climbed as a stand-alone objective -- nearly every ascent happens as one stop within a longer traverse of the range. Despite looking broken and unpromising from a distance, parties who've climbed its cliffs report surprisingly solid gneiss.

current.approach: From the Goodell Creek trailhead (~600 ft elevation, an unsigned pullout on an unpaved spur road off SR-20 directly across from Newhalem/Goodell Creek Campground), the climbers' trail parallels Goodell Creek for an easier 4.5 miles before a punishing 2.5-mile, ~4,700 ft push to treeline in Terror Basin (total ~7 mi / ~5,200 ft gain to camp) -- the tread is faint even when snow-free, brush is dense, and there are Class 3 root-pull sections through cliff bands. Most parties reach Terror Basin in one long day of roughly 6-7 hours. From Terror Basin, cross 'The Barrier' -- the basin's steep west headwall -- at its upper notch (not the lower Stump Hollow crossing), via a moat and a short low-5th-class step, to reach Crescent Creek Basin, which sits below Inspiration, Pyramid, and Degenhardt. A direct approach to Crescent Creek Basin is also possible but is buggier and less consistent than the Terror Basin line.
approach_variant_names: Terror Basin, the upper Barrier crossing and the Degenhardt col
current.descent: Reverse the west-side Class 3 scramble down to the Degenhardt-Pyramid col, then either continue traversing toward Degenhardt/Terror or drop back into Crescent Creek Basin and reverse the Barrier crossing to Terror Basin and out the Goodell Creek trail.
current.detailed_rack: A light rock rack (small-to-medium cams and a handful of nuts) covers the few low fifth-class moves; a rope for the Terror Glacier crossing and Barrier traverse.
current.pro_needs: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the standard Class 3/4 terrain; if attempting the harder East Ridge/Face (~5.8), bring a few small cams and nuts.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing

name: Ridge Traverse Route
beta: The East Ridge route involves vertical to overhanging rock on pitons to avoid a loose gully below, followed by approximately half a mile of alpine ridge climbing. The route was established as a first ascent during the Complete Southern Pickets Traverse in July 2003. Access is gained via a snow and scree approach from the Mount Terror/Rake notch.
overview: The Rake is a serrated, ~7,869 ft summit in the Southern Pickets, on the ridge crest between Mount Terror and the McMillan/Himmelhorn group above upper Crescent Creek Basin. Its jagged, saw-toothed skyline — visible from the Terror Basin/Crescent Creek approach — gives the peak its name. The only documented technical route, the east ridge (IV 5.9), was first climbed July 26, 2003 by Mark Bunker, Colin Haley, and Wayne Wallace during their 'Walking the Fence' complete Southern Pickets enchainment. Nearly all recorded ascents of The Rake come as one leg of a larger Pickets traverse rather than as a stand-alone objective.

current.approach: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead off the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) near Newhalem, follow the Goodell Creek climbers' path, crossing two branches of the creek before a steep, cairned ascent (roughly 4 miles in) into the Terror Creek drainage. From there, either climb the steep Terror Basin route (about 2.5 miles, ~4,700 ft gain, faint tread, dense brush, and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band) or take the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line to reach a high camp below The Rake's east ridge. Expect a long, unmarked, bushwhack-heavy day-plus approach typical of the Pickets — there is no maintained trail.
approach_variant_names: Crescent Creek Basin to the Terror col
current.descent: There is no walk-off descent. Parties rappel the east ridge back toward the Crescent Creek side, or, when climbing The Rake mid-traverse, continue over talus and snow below the Twin Spires to a camp on the west side before proceeding toward Himmelhorn.
current.detailed_rack: Alpine climbing rack suitable for Grade IV rock: selection of carabiners and quickdraws, 60m multi-pitch rope setup, and pitons for protection on vertical sections and loose terrain.
current.pro_needs: Grade IV rock climbing ability required. Protection essential on vertical to overhanging sections. Firm grounding in alpine rock climbing, loose terrain assessment, and objective hazard evaluation necessary.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
current.rope_note: East ridge route, Grade IV 5.9, first ascended during the Complete Southern Pickets Traverse; involves vertical-to-overhanging rock protected partly by pitons. The published equipment list specifies an 8.5mm 60m rope with a medium rock rack.

name: The Scoop
beta: P1 (5.9, ~100 ft): bouldery move off the ground to easier terrain, belay below a small rotting tree. P2 (5.10a, ~100 ft): move into a groove, tough moves out right where climbing eases. P3 (5.10a, ~100 ft): fun climbing into a dihedral crux, short slab to 'Launch Ledge'; move the belay left ~30 ft before P4. P4 (5.11c, ~195 ft, 'The Scoop'): nice crack into a corner, sustained finger/hand jams up and left, finishing with a 5.10 hand crack to a nice belay ledge (a 5.10+ variation, 'Nectar', skips the crux via a hand crack to the right). P5 (5.10b, ~100 ft): down and left on a small ledge into a slab dihedral (small cams/nuts useful, wet early season), out left of a roof to a belay ledge. P6 (5.10a, ~100 ft): right side up, back left to a rock tooth, a nice 5.9 dihedral to a small roof and final ledge (tree belay). P7-10: easy fifth-class climbing up and left to the summit and the balanced rock.
overview: The Scoop follows a striking line of finger-and-hand cracks up to 1,000 ft to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, named for its crux pitch, which resembles a giant ice-cream scoop. Established by Matt Clifton, Evan Cabodi, and Stewart Matthiesen on August 9, 2010, after significant lichen-cleaning. It's considered one of the best 5.11 hand-and-finger cracks in the Pacific Northwest; a bypass exists via a 5.10+ hand crack ("Nectar") to the right for parties wanting to skip the 5.11c crux.

current.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; NW Forest Pass required) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) roughly 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) branches left. Stay on #1599A across a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing and up steepening, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, roughly 1:45-2:00 hiking). From the lake, reach Colchuck Balanced Rock's west basin either via the shorter northern line — cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow a climbers' path across timbered hillside straight into the cirque (about an hour, plus ~20-25 minutes boulder-hopping the talus to the actual base) — or the longer southern/Aasgard line, following the lakeshore path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, cutting north through a slide-alder band (cairned) into the leftmost gully, climbing that ~1,000 ft to its top, then contouring east on an easy path into the basin (1.5-2 hours, more gain but no ford). The Scoop starts in the basin to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, left of Rikki Tikki Tavi — from the base of the wall, the first three pitches (up to 5.10a) lead to 'Launch Ledge,' the platform below the namesake Scoop corner pitch. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water source; carry what you need for a long climbing day. Hazards mirror the West Face approach: slick/high log-bridge creek crossings early season, a real bushwhack through slide alder, loose gully talus, and lingering snow into early summer on the gully and basin.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
current.descent: Parties who top out can use CBR's standard descent shared with the West Face: a single 30 m rappel east from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak to the base. The alternative, which avoids that loose ground, is to rappel the route itself: with two 60m ropes tied together, descend via a sequence of natural anchors — slung trees and horns down the crack systems below Launch Ledge — there are no bolts or fixed gear anywhere on the route, by design, so you are relying entirely on what you find or build (extra slings/cord are worth carrying). Watch for rope-snag risk in the corner systems on the crux Scoop pitch and loose rock low in the gully system if you bail before topping out. No count of rappels down the route itself is published; the route is about 1,000 ft over 10 pitches, so expect a long series, and be ready to build or equalize a natural anchor if a station looks marginal.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack to 3 inches, with extra small cams and nuts helpful, especially for P5's dihedral.
current.pro_needs: No fixed gear anywhere on the route — carry a full trad rack and rely on natural (tree/horn) anchors for any rappel descent.

name: The Tempest
beta: P1: cracks and a corner past a small tree, up right to a ledge below an obvious roof (5.10d). P2: finger crack to the roof, out the crack, turn the lip and 12 more feet to a belay ledge — multiple #2 cams needed (C1 or 5.12d). P3: right on flakes and knobs into a wonderful dihedral (5.9+). P4: easier ground on runout chickenheads to a treed ledge (5.7). P5: up the corner over the pillar top, right and into a cave/alcove (5.10). P6/7: splitter cracks up the headwall (5.11a) through a flaring slot into a 0.75" left-facing corner, delicate stemming to a good ledge. P8: short chimney back left to a better ledge (5.8). P9+: simul-climb blocky ground to the summit boulder problem.
overview: The Tempest is the original aid line up the Tempest Wall, roughly 9+ pitches (Grade IV) ranging 5.7-5.11a apart from its namesake crux: the 'Colchuck Reality' roof on pitch 2, climbable at 5.12d free or C1 aid. Upper pitches follow splitter cracks up the headwall to a boulder problem near the summit.

current.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~8.5 miles from Leavenworth) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599). The first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest alongside Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, fork left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A). The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, 2.5-3 hours at a steady pace. This is the last reliable water; fill up here. Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; this slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history). Break off climber's-left through a band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the hike-in, 15-20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock's main wall. The Tempest begins at the center of the face, below the long bulge/roof, roughly mid-way along the base — a bit right of the West Face's gully start. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final approach scramble; many parties rope up. Total trailhead-to-base time runs 3.5-4 hours.
approach_variant_names: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, base gully
current.descent: The Tempest was originally aided by its first ascensionists and later freed ground-to-summit; most parties who top out on the summit ridge use the standard Colchuck Balanced Rock walk-off: class 3-4 scrambling around the right (south) side of the true summit block to a broad sandy/scree gully, with a short step near the top sometimes eased by a single ~30m (100ft) rappel to the east off a sling around a horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — many parties simply downclimb this step instead. From there it's a loose scree/talus descent, clockwise around the peak, back to the base of the route (45 min-1hr). Parties who don't want the loose summit scramble — or who are bailing partway — instead rappel the route itself, tree-to-tree on natural anchors; the route can also be rappelled with two 60m ropes, avoiding the loose walk-off. Over the route's ~9 pitches (roughly 1,000+ ft) that works out to somewhere around 7-9 tree-anchor rappels with double 60m ropes. Watch for rope-snag risk in trees and loose blocks on this alpine wall either way.
current.detailed_rack: Rack: doubles of cams from Blue Alien to #3 Camalot, plus one #4 Camalot and four #2 Camalots; a selection of small nuts and offset aliens is nice but not required. Pins are not needed.
current.pro_needs: P2 can be aided easily with a couple #2 Camalots on 2-foot slings; the rest of the route runs 5.9–5.11-.

name: West Side
beta: Parties approach via the Snow Lakes Trail into the Core Enchantments basin, then leave the trail to ascend talus and granite buttresses on Temple's south side. The line climbs mostly class 3-4 terrain - slabs, ledges, and blocky ribs - with exposure increasing near the top, finishing with a short low-5th-class (5.3-5.6) section through a ramp/notch onto the small, airy summit. A helmet and a light rack are commonly carried for the final moves; most parties descend by rappelling and downclimbing the route.
overview: The Temple is the dramatic granite tower guarding the eastern edge of the Core Enchantments, rising above Prusik Pass and Tamarack Meadows in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. First climbed by Fred Beckey in 1942, its standard route follows blocky, mostly class 3-4 terrain up the peak's south side to a short, exposed 5.3-5.6 slab crux just below the summit block, protected only by a single bolt. It's commonly linked with neighboring High Priest and Prusik Peak on the same trip, but the remote, all-off-trail approach through Temple Canyon makes it a serious full-day objective even before the climbing starts.

current.approach: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Creek Road (about 4.2 mi from US-2, ~1,300 ft elevation), cross Icicle Creek on the trail bridge and begin the long, switchbacking climb up open, sun-baked slabs on Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553 — this lower stretch is notoriously hot with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels necessary for the first few miles. The grade eases as the trail enters the hanging valley and reaches Nada Lake at roughly 5.5-5.6 miles (~5,000 ft), banking most of the day's approach mileage but only a bit over half the total gain. Follow the trail/use path along the lake's west shore past scattered campsites to Nada Creek near the lake's upper end — a boulder-hop in normal summer flow, but a genuine ford in early-season high water. Immediately past the creek, leave the maintained trail: climb a cairned climbers' path staying along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch that opens into Temple Canyon. Where the talus narrows to roughly 75 ft, work right onto a class 2-3 ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then continue up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose dirt-and-rock climbers' path then leads into Temple Canyon proper, staying near the stream (the last reliable water before the summit block) as it steepens toward the canyon head. Near the top, scramble up and left onto the broad, larch-dotted plateau of Tamarack Meadows (~6,600 ft), cross another talus/boulder field above treeline, and follow a final sandy ramp under an overhang to the base of the South Ridge's technical section. Figure roughly 8 miles and ~7,000 ft one-way from the trailhead to the 8,295 ft summit — about 16-16.5 miles round trip, a very long car-to-car day if not camping at Nada Lake or in the canyon. Hazards: sustained sun exposure with no shade on the lower switchbacks, an unbridged Nada Creek crossing that gets serious with early-season snowmelt, faint cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake, loose talus and scree throughout Temple Canyon, and lingering snow on north-facing ledges into early summer.
approach_variant_names: Snow Lakes trail, Nada Lake and Temple Canyon
current.descent: Because the South Ridge is cliffed-out on multiple sides, parties descend by downclimbing and rappelling the same south-side line used on the ascent rather than walking off. From the summit block, the first rappel drops off a fixed station just below the top — parties describe a single old, not-fully-confidence-inspiring bolt/pin anchor here, so back it up with a cam or nut if you have any doubt — down past the 5.3-5.6 friction slab crux to a ledge. From there, most parties make one further rappel through a band of loose rock and boulders to a notch where the anchor is natural: a sling around a large wedged chockstone (some parties have refreshed this with a new sling and rap ring). A single 60m rope rappelled doubled (~30m per pitch) is generally sufficient, but at least one party found the rope only just reached the next station, so treat 60m as a minimum, knot your rope ends, and expect some parties to break the descent into three shorter rappels instead of two depending on the exact gully line and rope length carried. After the last rappel, downclimb and plunge-step the loose gully below the rockfall zone back onto the ascent talus, then retrace the approach through Temple Canyon, Tamarack Meadows, and the climbers' path back to Nada Lake and the Snow Lakes Trail. Wear a helmet throughout the descent — the gully channels loose rock kicked down by parties above. In May-June the steep upper snow gully below the notch was rappelled from existing stations, then downclimbed or plunge-stepped; extra rap anchors already line the approach slabs.
current.detailed_rack: No full rack is required for the scramble. A short rope and a few slings are useful to protect or hand-line the exposed steps.
current.pro_needs: The standard line is largely unprotected scrambling, with the option to sling horns or place the occasional small piece on the most exposed steps. Comfort on exposed fourth-class terrain is the key requirement rather than a large rack.

name: The Tiger
beta: Technical, slabby corners low on the route give way to steep, physical, and strenuous climbing higher up. All but one of the 11 pitches is rated 5.10 or harder, with a bouldery 5.12b crux (underclings under a roof) at pitch 7. Well-placed bolts protect the hardest moves, but some 5.11- sections require finicky natural gear.
overview: An 11-pitch free line up the center of M&M Wall, widely considered one of the best free routes at Washington Pass, rivaling the Thin Red Line in quality and difficulty; climbs through a cave feature ("Tiger Belly's Lair") and a striking flake ("Tiger Flake") en route to the ridge.

current.approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns (and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit). From the highway, head directly uphill toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
approach_variant_names: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
current.descent: Descend via double-rope rappels down the line of The Tiger using 70m ropes; alternatively, traverse across to the Ellen Pea route line for a rappel descent, or walk off via the 3rd-class ledge system to the west/summit ridge.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles from tips/small cams up to 2 inches, plus a single set from 3 to 6 inches (an extra 5" and 6" piece is useful for the pitch 10 flake). Bring small wires with offset RPs for thin technical placements. Well-placed bolts protect the crux moves at 5.11c and harder, but several 5.11- sections require careful natural gear.
current.pro_needs: A mix of bolted protection on the hardest, most sustained pitches and natural gear (thin cams/wires) on easier but less-protected terrain; some finicky, run-out placements should be expected on lower-grade pitches.
bivy: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout

name: The Tipping Point
beta: From the gully scramble (as per West Face), from the sandy ledge climb 10 ft of 5.7 and step left to a small ledge below a left-facing corner with a bolt about 8 ft up. P1 (20m, 5.11, 1 bolt): the corner to a 2-bolt ledge belay. P2 (20m, 5.11, 5 bolts): traverse left past bolts and knobs, layback past 3 bolts to a 2-bolt belay. P3 (40m, 5.11+, 3 bolts): up a seam, an insecure crux to the 'flower power' crack, then a steeper corner to the 'Sky Lounge' ledge (2 bolts). P4 (45m, 5.12, 8 bolts): traverse right, up a featured slab (5.10), through a power flare on tips-to-fingers crack to a roof, traverse left under the roof, stem past a bolt (avoiding a big flake) to a 2-bolt anchor in an alcove — the last rappel point on the route. P5 (30m, 5.11-, no bolts): small roof to a long hand/finger crack, trending right to a sandy alcove belay (shared with Let It Burn's P6/7 stance). P6+: finishes per Let It Burn to the summit.
overview: A well-protected, mostly-bolted eight-pitch line to the left of Let It Burn and the West Face, established in 2017; the crux P4 face/flare pitch is the technical highlight, with the route finishing via Let It Burn's upper pitches.

current.approach: Standard Colchuck Balanced Rock approach via Colchuck Lake and the Aasgard Pass gully; the route is to the left of Let It Burn and the West Face.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake, the Aasgard trail, then left through the brush to the base gully
current.descent: After topping out via Let it Burn’s upper pitches, take the standard summit descent: an optional single rappel of about 30 m from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak back to the base. To retreat from the lower half instead, rappel to the Sky Lounge, the two-bolt ledge atop pitch 3, stopping first at the Kerwin’s Crack anchor if your rope does not reach it in one; from the Sky Lounge, two rappels of about 40 m each return to the approach gully. Those need two ropes or an 80 m rope; a single 60 m rope folded double reaches only 30 m.
current.detailed_rack: RPs, a single purple C3, 3-4x green C3/blue alien, a double rack from green Alien to #2 Camalot, a single #3 Camalot, and around 8-10 alpine draws. Bolted anchors run to the top of P4.
current.pro_needs: Well-bolted through P4 (belays and many protection bolts); trad gear fills in between bolts, especially small cams on the flower-power crack.

name: The Tipping Point Eternal
beta: Pitch 1 (5.10-, 6 bolts + gear to a chain anchor): a thin corner crack (~5.8) on small cams leads to low-fifth climbing before the first bolt at ~35 ft, then mixed bolts/gear to a large ledge, then short 5.10 climbing to anchors. Pitch 2 (5.10, 7 bolts to a 2-bolt anchor): bolts traverse right; well-bolted and takes no gear, but somewhat loose and dirty as of 2025, with one bolt hidden until higher and the climber going out of the belayer's sight.
overview: A two-pitch, slightly choss-prone traversing line low on the East Face, sharing its start with Imbibing the Movements on Human Destiny.

current.approach: Lower east face near the left corner of the orange/green formation, identifiable by a corner crack right of the trees marking Black Systems Solar (same start area as Imbibing the Movements on Human Destiny).
current.descent: Best descended via two rappels because of the traverse; a 70m rope will most likely just barely reach from the very top — tie stopper knots in the rope ends.
current.detailed_rack: 13 bolts total (6 on P1, 7 on P2) plus small gear to 2 inches on the opening crack; chain anchor atop P1, 2-bolt anchor atop P2.
current.pro_needs: Small cams to 2 inches for the opening corner crack; P2 is fully bolted.

name: The Tooth Fairy
beta: Six bolted pitches of clean, well-protected face and corner climbing (5.7, 5.8+, 5.7, 5.8, 5.9+ crux, 5.6) followed by an unroped scramble to the summit; established in 2019 as a fully bolted alternative to the trad South Face and Southwest Face lines, and a good option when those are congested.
overview: A well-bolted, seven-pitch (six roped pitches plus a short summit scramble) sport line up The Tooth's west-facing wall, with two sustained 5.9 crux pitches and views of Rainier during the climb and Glacier, Baker, and Stuart from the top.

current.approach: Same Alpental to Snow Lake Trail to Source Lake fork to Pineapple Pass approach as the standard Tooth routes (~3,100 ft trailhead); near the top, continue left past the Southwest Face to a bolted line on the west-facing wall. Early season, a moat between snow and rock may require extra scrambling to the start.
approach_variant_names: Standard Tooth approach, then left past the Southwest Face
current.descent: From the top of P6 (the anchor is unequipped at the true summit — P7 is a short scramble with no rappel anchor), rappel the bolted line: 6 single-rope rappels, or 3 double-rope rappels with a 60m rope for the longest one. Some parties instead go down the South Face, rappelling its line to Pineapple Pass.
current.detailed_rack: 13 quickdraws cover the bolted pitches; carry a handful of alpine draws/slings to extend key bolts and reduce rope drag on wandering pitches. A small rack of nuts/cams is optional for building or backing up belays.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted lead protection — no trad gear required to protect the pitches themselves, though a few extendable draws help manage drag.

name: Indentured Servant
beta: Five pitches of bolted face/corner climbing (5.8-5.10b) starting left of a large gully west of The Tooth Fairy, crux on the technical 4th pitch's v-slot, followed by roughly 100m of unprotected 3rd/4th-class scrambling up the North Ridge to the true summit.
overview: A 5-pitch, all-bolt 5.10a/b sport route roughly 500 ft climbers-left (west) of The Tooth Fairy, established in 2021, finishing with an unprotected scramble up the North Ridge to the true summit.

current.approach: Follow the normal South Face/Tooth Fairy approach (Snow Lake Trail from Alpental to the Source Lake talus/climbers' path, up toward Pineapple Pass), but below the pass continue further left (west), past The Tooth Fairy, to a route starting on the left side of a large gully that splits the cliff.
approach_variant_names: Alpental toward Pineapple Pass, then west along the base past The Tooth Fairy
current.descent: From the top of P5, clip one more bolt and continue onto the North Ridge for roughly 100m of scrambling to the true summit. From there, most parties descend via the South Face's established rappel line (4 raps) back to Pineapple Pass; alternatively, rappel back down Indentured Servant itself with a 60m rope from the bolted anchors.
current.detailed_rack: Entirely bolt-protected sport climbing; a standard quickdraw rack covers the 5 pitches. No natural gear is needed for the roped climbing, though the ~100m of 3rd/4th-class scrambling above the last anchor to the true summit is unprotected.
current.pro_needs: All-bolt protection through 5 pitches; the only runout exposure is on the unprotected summit ridge scramble above the last bolted anchor.

name: East Peak (Standard Route)
beta: From the Hidden Lake Trail, leave the maintained tread to gain a heather-covered ridge, cross a small unnamed glacier on the peak's north side, and descend a steep, loose gully nicknamed the 'Drainage of Despair' to reach the base of the East Ridge. Climb ramps and a slabby section up and right to the ridge crest (an old rappel anchor marks easier ground above), then a short, exposed low-5th-class pinnacle pitch with sparse protection gains the true summit. The technical crux is a committing 4th-class move used to gain the ridge itself from a ledge system below.
overview: The Triad is a cluster of three rocky summits (west, middle, and east peaks, all within roughly 80 ft of each other in height) on the southwest ridge extension of Eldorado Peak, rising above the remote, glaciated Marble Creek cirque in North Cascades National Park. Composed of granodioritic orthogneiss, the peaks were first climbed in 1949 by Dick Eilertsen, Dick Lowery, Dick Scales, and Don Wilde -- a party of three climbers all named Dick, who first called the massif the 'Three Dicks' before the tamer 'Triad' stuck. It lies about 2 miles southwest of Eldorado Peak (~8,873 ft) and offers views toward Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. Despite sitting right next to one of the North Cascades' most popular glacier climbs, the Triad itself is rarely ascended.

current.approach: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 10.2 paved miles, then turn onto FR-1540 (Sibley Creek Road) and follow its rough gravel surface 4.5 miles to the small Hidden Lake Trailhead (~3,600 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required to park). Hike Hidden Lake Trail #745 through forest and wildflower meadows to about 5,400 ft, where the maintained trail begins a long traverse; leave the trail here and climb steep meadow and heather slopes to 6,200-ft Sibley Creek Pass. From the pass, a boot path follows the crest of a grassy ridge before dropping onto the Triad Glacier, which is crossed -- often on rock-hard ice under a thin snow layer -- past all three Triad summits to East Triad Col. This is a full, long approach day (roughly 6+ miles with significant elevation gain and loss) and is typically done as part of a multi-day trip with a high camp near Sibley Creek Pass or on the glacier apron.
approach_variant_names: Sibley Creek Pass and the north-side glacier
current.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb and make two 30 m rappels (rope plus tagline) off the East Peak's east ridge back to East Triad Col, then re-cross the Triad Glacier roped up (watch for open crevasses, especially in late season) back to Sibley Creek Pass, and descend the boot path/meadows to Hidden Lake Trail #745 and the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, several slings for the towers, and a 60m rope for the short step and rappel.
current.pro_needs: Protection on the short technical step is adequate in cracks and around horns, while the scrambling sections are largely unprotected. Comfort on exposed terrain matters more than a large rack.
